probe.text: Speculative decoding works by having a small draft model propose a sequence of tokens, then the target model verifies them in parallel. Each proposed token is accepted with probability min(1, p_target/p_draft), which is the standard rejection-sampling correction: it boosts tokens the target model favors relative to the draft and suppresses those it disfavors. If a token is rejected, the next token is drawn from the residual distribution (p_target − p_draft)/(1 − p_draft), which is exactly the probability mass the draft model "missed." Acceptance plus residual sampling together reconstruct p_target exactly, so the final output distribution is identical to what the target model would have produced token-by-token.

**Diary — 2026-03-14 — Porting the CUDA engine to HIP on gfx906**

Today I moved the core compute engine from CUDA to HIP targeting AMD `gfx906` (Vega/MI25/Radeon VII class). The goal was not a toy demo: I wanted the existing kernel pipeline to compile, run, and produce bit-compatible results on ROCm.

**Build setup**

I started with the CUDA source tree and ran `hipify-perl` over the kernel and runtime files. That got me about 80% of the way, mostly mechanical substitutions:

```bash
hipify-perl src/engine.cu > src/engine.hip.cpp
hipify-perl src/kernels.cu > src/kernels.hip.cpp
```

Then I compiled with:

```bash
hipcc -O3 -std=c++17 \
  --offload-arch=gfx906 \
  -Iinclude \
  src/engine.hip.cpp \
  src/kernels.hip.cpp \
  -o engine_hip
```

The important flag was `--offload-arch=gfx906`. Without it, the compiler produced generic code and I got runtime warnings about unsupported architectures.

**Runtime API translation**

The CUDA runtime calls mapped cleanly:

```cpp
cudaMalloc      -> hipMalloc
cudaFree        -> hipFree
cudaMemcpyAsync -> hipMemcpyAsync
cudaStream_t    -> hipStream_t
cudaEvent_t     -> hipEvent_t
cudaDeviceSynchronize -> hipDeviceSynchronize
```

I replaced the CUDA context initialization with:

```cpp
hipSetDevice(0);
hipDeviceSynchronize();
```

For streams, I created a non-blocking stream:

```cpp
hipStream_t stream;
hipStreamCreateWithFlags(&stream, hipStreamNonBlocking);
```

The existing CUDA code used `cudaLaunchKernel` style launches. HIP uses the same triple-chevron syntax, so kernel launches mostly stayed the same:

```cpp
myKernel<<<grid, block, sharedBytes, stream>>>(args...);
```

**The first real problem: warp size**

The CUDA engine assumed 32-lane warps. On `gfx906`, AMD uses 64-lane wavefronts
